data.title: BYD M9 lands from $61,990: Forget other Chinese people-movers, the M9 is aimed straight at the top-selling Kia Carnival
data.description:
BYD has put a sharp $61,990 plus on-road costs starting price on its new M9 plug-in hybrid people-mover, pitching the newcomer surprisingly close to mainstream rivals such as the top-selling Kia Carnival while significantly undercutting the latest crop of electrified Chinese people-movers.

The eight-seat M9 Dynamic will open the range at $61,990 plus ORCs, while the better-equipped seven-seat M9 Premium costs $72,990 plus ORCs.

The Premium will be the first into Australian showrooms in the coming months, with the Dynamic to follow later.

READ MORE: BYD adds yet another new model to its Aussie line-up: M9 to join the growing Chinese people-mover battle
READ MORE: History made! $19,990 BYD Atto 1 becomes Australia’s cheapest new car as EV price war hits new low
READ MORE: BYD’s smaller Shark breaks cover: New Mako PHEV ute revealed as potential Ford Maverick and Toyota rival

The pricing continues BYD’s increasingly aggressive approach to the Australian market, coming just days after the Atto 1 became Australia’s cheapest new car with a sub-$20,000 drive-away offer.

The M9 will become BYD’s first Australian people-mover and its seventh all-new model launched locally within 12 months as the Chinese brand continues its rapid expansion into new segments as it seeks market domination.

The M9 pricing looks particularly competitive considering this is a large plug-in hybrid people-mover rather than a conventional petrol or diesel model.

The cheapest Kia Carnival is the $54,560 plus-ORCs S diesel, while the Carnival S Hybrid starts at $56,310. At the other end of the range, the GT-Line Hybrid costs $76,840.

That means the entry M9 costs only $5680 more than the cheapest Carnival hybrid, while the better-equipped M9 Premium is $3850 cheaper than the flagship Carnival hybrid.

The M9 also significantly undercuts the latest wave of electrified Chinese people-movers entering Australia.

The GAC M8 plug-in hybrid starts at $76,590 plus ORCs, while the battery-electric Denza D9 opens at $88,185, the XPeng X9 at $89,900 and Zeekr 009 at $115,900.

Its price positioning will also give Chinese arch-rival GWM something to think about with the launch of its new premium brand Wey and the G9 people-mover coming soon.

Both M9 variants are front-wheel drive and employ BYD’s latest DM-i 5.0 plug-in hybrid system, combining a 1.5-litre turbo-petrol engine with a single front electric motor. There is no rear motor or all-wheel drive.

BYD has so far released detailed Australian specifications only for the Premium, with full specifications for the cheaper Dynamic to come later.

What is confirmed is a significant difference in battery capacity. The Premium uses a 36.6kWh BYD Blade battery, while the Dynamic gets a smaller 20.39kWh unit.

In Premium specification the M9 produces a combined maximum 218kW. Its petrol engine develops 315Nm, while the front electric motor produces 300Nm, and BYD claims 0-100km/h in 8.5 seconds.

The Premium has a claimed 145km WLTP electric range and up to 850km of combined petrol-electric range.

There are some interesting fuel consumption numbers in BYD’s own Australian documentation.

The detailed specification sheet lists WLTP combined consumption at 2.4L/100km and 7.3L/100km when the battery reaches a critical state of charge, as well as CO2 emissions of 9g/km.

However, the front page of the same Australian brochure advertises fuel consumption of “from 0.4L/100km” with sufficient battery state of charge, also described as a WLTP combined-cycle result.

The Premium can charge at up to 85kW DC or 7kW AC, with BYD claiming an 18-minute 30-80 per cent DC recharge. Vehicle-to-load (V2L) output is rated at up to 6kW.

The M9 is a substantial machine, measuring 5145mm long, 1970mm wide and 1805mm high on a 3045mm wheelbase.

The Premium weighs 2650kg and has a 3374kg gross vehicle mass, while luggage capacity is 470 litres with all three rows in use. Braked towing capacity is 1500kg.

It also gets BYD’s DiSus-C adaptive damping system and 18-inch wheels wearing Michelin e.Primacy tyres.

The seven-seat Premium uses a 2+2+3 configuration, with second-row captain’s chairs offering heating, ventilation, massage and a near zero-gravity seating position.

The driver also gets a massage function and both front seats are heated and ventilated.

Technology includes a 12.3-inch digital instrument display, 15.6-inch central infotainment touchscreen, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, over-the-air updates and four-zone voice control.

The Premium adds a 15.6-inch ceiling-mounted rear entertainment display and 12-speaker audio system, while an integrated refrigerator/hotbox can chill its contents to minus 6 degrees Celsius or heat them to 50 degrees.

Safety equipment includes up to nine airbags, a 360-degree camera, five millimetre-wave radars, eight ultrasonic sensors and an extensive suite of driver-assistance technology.

BYD says high-strength steel makes up 73 per cent of the M9’s structure.

The post BYD M9 lands from $61,990: Forget other Chinese people-movers, the M9 is aimed straight at the top-selling Kia Carnival appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Locked in for Australia: Geely confirms 830kW Toyota Prado rival and Monjaro PHEV family SUV as 2027 model blitz grows
data.description:
Geely has confirmed two significant new plug-in hybrid SUVs for Australia in 2027, including an 830kW Toyota Prado and Ford Everest rival that will be known locally as the Battleship 700.

The rugged Battleship 700 will arrive in the second half of 2027, while the more road-focused five-seat Monjaro EM-i family SUV is scheduled for the first half of the year.

Both are making their Australian public debut at this weekend’s Everything Electric show in Sydney alongside the previously confirmed Emgrand L EM-i plug-in hybrid sedan. Geely says the trio represents half of the six new models it plans to launch in Australia during 2027.

READ MORE: Another potential electric ute for Australia? Geely’s new Riddara King Kong EV takes aim at workhorse market
READ MORE: Another challenger for Toyota Camry: Geely Emgrand L EM-i PHEV confirmed for Australia in 2027
READ MORE: Geely Monjaro? Remember that name, because this big new family PHEV SUV is coming to Australia
READ MORE: Look out Denza B5, Toyota Prado and Ford Everest! Geely Galaxy Cruiser 700 is launching with an 830kW tri-motor plug-in powertrain

The announcement fills in some significant blanks in Geely’s aggressive Australian expansion plans. However, pricing remains a TBA.

The biggest news surrounds the Battleship 700, which is the production off-road SUV previously known as the Galaxy Cruiser 700.

Overseas, the Battleship 700 combines a 2.0-litre turbocharged four-cylinder petrol engine with a 47kWh battery and three electric motors, producing a claimed 830kW. Australian specification is expected to be very similar and will be confirmed closer to its launch.

That puts the Battleship into the rapidly expanding field of electrified off-road SUVs taking aim at established large 4x4s such as the Toyota Prado and Ford Everest, as well as newer PHEV rivals including the Denza B5.

The Australian announcement confirms a claimed electric-only range of up to 170km, although Geely stresses that final local specifications will not be announced until closer to launch.

The Battleship 700 rides on 20-inch wheels and has 233mm of ground clearance and an 800mm wading depth. There is also a so-called ‘Waltz’ U-Turn function designed to give the big SUV very tight low-speed manoeuvrability.

Inside, equipment detailed for the overseas model includes 12.3-inch and 15.6-inch displays, a panoramic sunroof, separate rear air-conditioning, a heating and cooling compartment in the centre console and a 23-speaker audio system.

The Monjaro EM-i is a very different proposition, sitting above the existing Starray EM-i as a larger and more upmarket five-seat family SUV aimed at the likes of the Toyota Kluger and the many other mainstream and premium models competing in the large SUV segment.

Its Australian arrival in the first half of 2027 is now officially confirmed after Geely had previously revealed only that a larger five-seat SUV was on its way.

Built on Geely’s newer GEA EVO architecture, the Monjaro combines a 1.5-litre turbocharged four-cylinder petrol engine with two electric motors and a battery of up to 40kWh.

Geely is claiming as much as 170km of electric driving range and 1137km combined range on the WLTP cycle. Front- and all-wheel-drive configurations will be offered internationally, along with 19- and 20-inch wheels.

The Monjaro also gets Continuously Controlled Damping suspension and chassis tuning by Geely Technology Europe.

Cabin equipment includes a 15.4-inch central touchscreen, 25.6-inch ultra-wide head-up display, surround-view camera, heated, ventilated and massaging front seats and heated rear seats. Vehicle-to-load and vehicle-to-vehicle capability of up to 6.6kW is also included.

The Monjaro name has been used internationally since 2021 for export versions of the Chinese-market Xingyue L, but this latest EM-i version is a substantial technical change, moving to Geely’s newer electrified architecture and plug-in hybrid drivetrain.

Geely’s third 2027 model on display in Sydney is the Emgrand L EM-i sedan, which was already confirmed for Australia earlier this month.

The three models form part of an unusually rapid expansion for Geely, which only returned to Australia as a factory-backed brand in 2025.

Its local range currently spans the EX5 electric SUV, EX2 electric hatch and Starray EM-i PHEV SUV, with more models due next year.

That expansion is being backed by rapidly increasing sales. Geely recorded 4504 Australian deliveries in August, placing it ninth among brands for the month. The EX5 contributed 1947 sales, while the EX2 and Starray EM-i recorded 1279 and 1278 respectively.

Geely says the Monjaro EM-i, Emgrand L EM-i and Battleship 700 account for three of six models it plans to launch in Australia during 2027, meaning another three vehicles remain to be fully detailed.

Geely is already taking $200 holding deposits for the Monjaro EM-i and Emgrand L EM-i until September 30. Customers are offered a complimentary EV home charger and premium paint upgrade, while Monjaro AWD customers are also offered a suede-like upholstery upgrade.

The post Locked in for Australia: Geely confirms 830kW Toyota Prado rival and Monjaro PHEV family SUV as 2027 model blitz grows appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Is this the anti-Toyota HiLux EV dual-cab ute? MG U9 electric ute priced from $78,990 with 430km range and 3.5-tonne towing
data.description:
MG has priced its new U9 EV at $78,990 plus on-road costs, putting the electric ute directly up against the Toyota HiLux BEV, but with a dramatically different set of priorities.

The U9 EV costs just $2500 more than the $76,490 plus ORCs HiLux SR BEV pick-up and $4000 less than the $82,990 HiLux SR5 BEV, making the comparison between Australia’s two new electric utes difficult to avoid.

At $78,990 plus on-road costs, the U9 EV also carries a substantial premium over its diesel-powered stablemates, which are priced from $52,990 to $60,990 drive-away. That puts the EV $18,000 above even the most expensive diesel U9 before its on-road costs are added.

Beyond price and their dual-cab bodies, MG and Toyota have taken markedly different approaches.

READ MORE: Why the MG U9 could be the first electric dual cab ute Aussie buyers will take seriously
READ MORE: Global debut: Chinese PHEV ute avalanche continues with MG U9 dual cab 4×4 rival for BYD Shark 6, GWM Cannon Alpha and Ford Ranger PHEV
READ MORE: Fightback: Huge campaign rolled out for MG and IM as struggling Chinese giant stakes its Aussie future on EVs

While Australia’s number-one new-car brand is targeting its first electric ute primarily at business and fleet customers, MG openly describes the U9 EV as a “lifestyle ute”, aimed at buyers towing caravans and boats, carrying recreational equipment and using their ute as a family vehicle.

And the specifications underline that difference. The $78,990 MG packs a 102.2kWh battery, 430km WLTP range, 3500kg braked towing capacity and a 325kW/700Nm dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain.

The HiLux BEV uses a much smaller 59.2kWh battery, produces 144kW and is rated to tow 2000kg braked, reflecting Toyota’s emphasis on commercial and back-to-base use rather than long-distance recreational driving.

That bigger battery and towing capacity come with compromises. The MG has a relatively modest 685kg payload, while its maximum 115kW DC charging rate is actually lower than the Toyota’s 150kW peak.

Four-wheel electronic air suspension is also standard, further underlining the U9’s comfort-oriented positioning.

One area where the Toyota has a clear specification advantage is DC charging. The HiLux can accept up to 150kW and Toyota claims approximately 30 minutes for a 10-80 per cent recharge. Despite its much larger battery, the MG is limited to 115kW and requires a claimed 42 minutes to charge from 20-80 per cent.

The U9 EV supports 11kW AC charging and also offers substantial vehicle-to-load capability, with up to 6.6kW available through the external CCS2 outlet and three additional 2.2kW outlets inside the cabin.

Storage includes a sizeable 236-litre front boot, while MG says the rear tub can accommodate a standard pallet. A hands-free powered tailgate is also fitted.

The lifestyle theme continues inside with dual 12.3-inch screens, leather front seats, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, 15W wireless phone charging and an eight-speaker JBL sound system.

The driver’s seat is heated and ventilated and includes massage functionality, while the front passenger seat and steering wheel are also heated.

A 360-degree camera system is included and MG says the U9 EV has achieved a five-star ANCAP safety rating.

MG Motor Australia says the vehicle has been designed and tested with Australian usage in mind.

“The MGU9 EV brings together the capability and utility people expect from a ute with the comfort and benefits of an electric powertrain,” said MG Motor Australia marketing director Dimitri Andreatidis.

“It’s designed to be used every day, whether that’s for work during the week, the school run or getting away on the weekend.”

MG U9 EV v Toyota HiLux BEV specifications

The post Is this the anti-Toyota HiLux EV dual-cab ute? MG U9 electric ute priced from $78,990 with 430km range and 3.5-tonne towing appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Wey forward: New Chinese brand gains Aussie sales approval for PHEV and hybrid G9 people-mover
data.description:
GWM’s new luxury Wey brand has surfaced in Australia ahead of its showroom launch, with its first model approved for local sale.

The seven-seat GWM Wey G9 people mover has appeared in Australian Government homologation documents with both plug-in hybrid and conventional hybrid powertrains, ahead of its expected introduction before the end of 2026.

The filing is another concrete step towards the arrival of Wey, which will join GWM’s existing Haval, Tank, Cannon and Ora brands in Australia and is being positioned as a rival for BYD’s premium Denza marque.

READ MORE: It’s another giant Chinese PHEV SUV! And the GWM Wey V9X is a real chance to come to Australia
READ MORE: Wey the latest Chinese brand to announce Aussie launch: GWM goes upmarket
READ MORE: GWM plans Aussie model onslaught as it gets the keys to the brand’s entire product portfolio

The G9 will make a relatively low-key debut because of the small scale of the Australian people-mover market, before Wey expands into higher-volume SUV segments during 2027.

The Road Vehicle Descriptor (RVD) identifies the vehicle internally as the M81 and gives its Australian marketing designation as the GWM Wey G9.

Known as the Gaoshan in China and Wey 80 in some export markets, the G9 is a substantial vehicle measuring 5055mm long, 1985mm wide and 1925mm high, with a 3085mm wheelbase and seven seats.

The first of the two Australian-approved versions is an all-wheel drive PHEV combining a 1.5-litre turbocharged four-cylinder petrol engine with front and rear electric motors and a six-speed DHT transmission.

The RVD lists the PHEV powertrain at 325kW. It has a hefty 2759kg tare mass and 3355kg gross vehicle mass, while the homologation documents currently list zero braked and unbraked towing capacity.

However, the bigger surprise is the approval of a conventional hybrid G9 alongside the PHEV.

When GWM originally confirmed Wey for Australia, the plan was for the luxury brand to concentrate exclusively on PHEVs. Since then the G9 hybrid has become available internationally and is now expected to join the Australian line-up.

The HEV uses a 2.0-litre turbocharged four-cylinder petrol engine with electric assistance, all-wheel drive and a six-speed DHT. The RVD lists its output at 263kW.

At 2504kg, the hybrid is 255kg lighter than the PHEV and, unlike the plug-in version, is homologated to tow 1500kg braked and 750kg unbraked.

The addition of the HEV also indicates Wey’s Australian powertrain strategy is becoming more flexible. Rather than sticking rigidly to the original PHEV-only plan, other powertrains could be considered for future models depending on what becomes available.

The G9 will arrive later than initially anticipated, with GWM previously targeting a mid-2026 introduction for Wey. EV Central understands there is no specific problem behind the delay, which instead reflects the usual complexities of establishing a new brand and building its supporting dealer network.

That work continues ahead of a more substantial Wey push expected from early 2027. The large six-seat V9X SUV is expected to play a central role in that expansion, while the smaller V8X SUV is another potential Australian addition.

Those SUVs will give Wey access to much larger segments of the Australian market and provide a more direct challenge to Denza as the two Chinese luxury brands expand their local ranges.

For now, though, the G9 will have the job of introducing Wey to Australia. Pricing and final specifications have yet to be announced, but GWM has previously indicated Wey models would be positioned below $100,000.

The post Wey forward: New Chinese brand gains Aussie sales approval for PHEV and hybrid G9 people-mover appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Another electric van enters the fray: Hyundai Staria Load Electric lands at $70,990 with 450km range and ultra-fast charging
data.description:
Hyundai has priced its first battery-electric van for Australia, with the 2027 Hyundai Staria Load Electric arriving at $70,990 plus on-road costs and offering up to 450km of WLTP driving range.

The electric Staria Load sits at the top of Hyundai’s commercial van range, commanding a substantial premium over the $49,990 turbo-diesel and $53,490 hybrid versions, while also entering an increasingly competitive electric van market.

At $70,990 before on-road costs, the Staria Load Electric costs $21,000 more than the diesel and $17,500 more than the Staria Load Hybrid. It is also significantly more expensive than the $55,990 plus ORCs Kia PV5 Cargo, while current promotional pricing has pushed some other electric vans even lower.

READ MORE: Revealed and confirmed! Kia PV7 electric van locked in for Australia with 460km-plus range, ultra-fast charging and up to nine seats
READ MORE: A BEV at an ICE price: Ford Transit City electric van lands in Australia from $50,000 drive-away to take on the Toyota HiAce
READ MORE: LDV extends Australia’s cheapest electric van at $47,990 as eDeliver 7 gets huge $9000 discount

LDV is currently offering the larger eDeliver 7 from $54,990 drive-away for eligible ABN holders, while Volkswagen is advertising remaining MY25 ID. Buzz Cargo stock from $69,990 drive-away until the end of September.

At the other end of the spectrum, the Ford E-Transit Custom is positioned above the Hyundai, having launched at $77,890 plus ORCs.

But Hyundai is countering the Staria Load Electric’s relatively high entry price with some of the strongest range and charging figures in the class.

Its 84kWh battery feeds a 160kW/350Nm electric motor driving the front wheels and provides a claimed WLTP range of up to 450km. Hyundai quotes combined electricity consumption of 20.7kWh/100km.

More unusually for a commercial EV, the Staria Load Electric adopts an 800-volt electrical architecture and supports DC charging at up to 350kW. Hyundai claims a 10-80 per cent recharge can be completed in 20 minutes under suitable conditions.

That compares with a claimed 416km WLTP range for the Kia PV5 Cargo and 431km for the Volkswagen ID. Buzz Cargo, while the Ford E-Transit Custom offers up to 340km.

The Hyundai also retains the same 4935-litre cargo capacity as the diesel and hybrid Staria Load, with an internal load area measuring 2607mm long, 1640mm wide and 1436mm high.

Payload is rated at 1005kg, marginally higher than the diesel’s 997kg and just below the hybrid’s 1039kg.

Another significant point of difference is towing capacity. The Staria Load Electric is rated to tow up to 2000kg braked and 750kg unbraked, giving it substantially more trailer capability than many electric commercial vans.

An interior Vehicle-to-Load outlet is fitted in the cargo area, allowing the traction battery to supply electricity to tools and other equipment through a conventional three-pin outlet.

Hyundai is offering the Staria Load Electric exclusively as a two-seater, with buyers able to choose either a conventional liftback or Twin Swing rear doors at the same $70,990 price.

The EV also receives a 23.9-litre front storage compartment and specific measures aimed at improving refinement, including rack-mounted electric power steering, strut-mounted dynamic dampers and sound-absorbing tyres.

Standard equipment includes 12.3-inch multimedia and 12.3-inch digital instrument displays, satellite navigation, wireless phone charging, Hyundai Bluelink connected services, over-the-air software updates, a heat pump and battery heating system.

There are seven airbags and a suite of driver-assistance systems including autonomous emergency braking, blind-spot collision avoidance, rear cross-traffic collision avoidance, lane-keeping assistance, Lane Following Assist 2 and adaptive cruise control with stop-and-go functionality.

The electric model can be identified by its closed front panel, centrally mounted charging port, aerodynamic underbody covers and Electric badging. It rides on 17-inch steel wheels and is offered in Creamy White or Shimmering Silver.

Hyundai lists scheduled servicing for the Staria Load Electric at 30,000km intervals, with the first two services priced at $645 and $667 respectively.

The high-voltage battery is covered for eight years or 160,000km, although Hyundai’s broader warranty conditions differ for vehicles used in commercial applications.

2027 Hyundai Staria Load pricing

Staria Load 2.2 diesel: $49,990 plus ORCs
Staria Load Hybrid: $53,490 plus ORCs
Staria Load Hybrid Premium: $61,240 plus ORCs
Staria Load Electric: $70,990 plus ORCs

The post Another electric van enters the fray: Hyundai Staria Load Electric lands at $70,990 with 450km range and ultra-fast charging appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Hyundai’s battery breakthrough: Next-gen tech will back massive 100-model global launch program
data.description:
Hyundai is preparing a new generation of cheaper, faster-charging and longer-lasting batteries to underpin a massive global product offensive that will see more than 100 new or updated vehicles launched by the end of the decade.

The Korean auto giant has detailed an extensive battery development program that includes new in-house battery cells, a switch to significantly cheaper mid-nickel chemistry for upcoming EVs, smarter battery management and new technology designed to prevent thermal runaway spreading through a battery pack.

It comes as Hyundai prepares one of the largest product rollouts in its history, with more than 100 global launches and major model updates planned by 2030.

READ MORE: Revealed: Hyundai’s 1000km-plus electric ute tech will debut in Santa Fe SUV range extender
READ MORE: Hyundai Ioniq 3 priced: UK version of new EV rival for BYD and MG starts at $42,500 … that’s promising for Australia
READ MORE: Hyundai’s 1000km-plus electric ute delayed: It’s still coming to Australia but it could take until 2030 to get here

More than 18 will take Hyundai into new products or market segments and seven new vehicles are due within the next eight months alone.

The rollout will include conventional combustion-powered vehicles, hybrids, extended-range electric vehicles (EREVs) and battery-electric vehicles, with electrified models targeted to account for 60 per cent of Hyundai sales by 2030, up from 23 per cent in 2025.

Hyundai is targeting 5.55 million global vehicle sales and a six per cent global market share by the end of the decade.

Central to the technology push is Hyundai’s development of its own battery cells.

The company claims its new high-performance cells can produce more than twice the output of the high-nickel cells it has previously used while reducing charging time by 40 per cent.

The first application will be Hyundai’s new EREV powertrain arriving in the first half of 2027.

That system will initially appear in the new Santa Fe EREV, which Hyundai says will offer more than 600 miles – about 965km – of total driving range.

Hyundai says the EREV requires less than half the battery capacity of a comparable battery-electric vehicle while still providing equivalent battery performance and EV driving characteristics.

The technology is also significant for Australia because EREV is emerging as a leading candidate to power Hyundai’s upcoming body-on-frame midsize ute.

But Hyundai’s battery plans extend well beyond EREVs.

One of the biggest developments for conventional battery-electric vehicles will arrive from 2027.

Hyundai says EVs launching next year will adopt mid-nickel NCM – nickel-cobalt-manganese – battery cells that will reduce battery costs by around 30 per cent compared with the technology they replace.

Importantly, Hyundai claims the cheaper cells will maintain what it describes as “optimal performance” under real-world driving conditions.

The potential significance is substantial because the battery remains one of the most expensive individual components in an electric vehicle.

A 30 per cent reduction in battery cost does not mean the price of an entire Hyundai EV will fall by 30 per cent, but reducing the cost of the pack potentially gives the company much greater scope to lower vehicle prices – or fit larger batteries and more equipment without pushing prices higher.

It should also help Hyundai compete against the rapidly expanding number of lower-cost Chinese EV manufacturers.

The first models using the new mid-nickel batteries have not been identified.

However, they will arrive during an enormous expansion of Hyundai’s electrified range.

In Europe alone Hyundai plans to cover 85 per cent of the market with a fully electrified portfolio, including five new SUVs and light-commercial vehicles, while increasing annual EV sales from 116,000 in 2025 to more than 420,000 by 2030.

Hyundai isn’t concentrating purely on the chemistry inside the battery.

Software will increasingly be used to manage the battery throughout its working life.

Hyundai says an enhanced cloud-based battery management system (BMS) will extend the average life of its EV batteries by 20 per cent by 2028.

The system will monitor battery condition and use cloud connectivity to detect abnormalities in individual cells in real time.

That could have implications beyond how long owners can keep their cars.

Battery degradation and the cost of replacing an EV battery remain important considerations for used EV buyers, while improved battery longevity potentially increases residual values and extends the useful life of an electric vehicle.

Hyundai hasn’t detailed exactly how it has calculated its claimed 20 per cent average battery-life improvement or translated it into expected kilometres or years of service.

The other major component of Hyundai’s battery strategy is safety.

Hyundai has developed what it calls Thermal Runaway Protection (TRP), designed to prevent heat from a failing battery cell spreading into adjacent cells.

Thermal runaway occurs when a battery cell experiences an uncontrolled increase in temperature that can trigger further cells, potentially creating a chain reaction within the battery pack.

Rather than simply delaying the spread of heat, Hyundai claims its TRP system can block it at the source.

It combines a battery design that dissipates heat with barriers between individual cells intended to stop heat transfer.

Hyundai says the technology has been verified through more than 200 repeated tests using both prismatic and pouch-type NCM batteries.

The cloud-based BMS and TRP effectively provide two layers of defence.

The BMS is intended to detect abnormal behaviour early enough for preventative action to be taken, while TRP provides a physical defence against heat spreading if a cell does fail.

The new thermal-runaway technology will make its production debut with Genesis, with Hyundai’s roadmap identifying the upcoming electric GV90 flagship SUV as its first application.

The battery investment is part of a broader change in Hyundai’s electrification strategy.

Rather than relying exclusively on battery-electric vehicles, Hyundai is expanding across EVs, hybrids and EREVs as it pushes towards its 5.55-million annual sales target.

Among the models identified in the latest roadmap are the IONIQ 3, new-generation Tucson and Tucson Hybrid, Santa Fe EREV, a new electric SUV for India and new global and European B-segment SUVs.

Genesis will simultaneously expand beyond pure EVs with its first hybrid, the GV80 Hybrid, as well as an EREV SUV targeting more than 640 miles – around 1030km – of total range and the battery-electric GV90 flagship.

The post Hyundai’s battery breakthrough: Next-gen tech will back massive 100-model global launch program appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: What’s the deal with 800V? Why the EV tech that only matters some of the time should not be at the top of your shopping list
data.description:
Read a press kit for many new electric cars revealed recently and you could find a reference to 800 volts in it somewhere.

BMW’s new iX3 (pictured above). The Mercedes-Benz CLA. Porsche’s soon-to-arrive Cayenne Electric. Various cars from Zeekr, XPeng, Lotus and more.

Of course, the Porsche Taycan, Audi e-tron GT and various Kias and Hyundais have been using 800V architectures for years.

But recently the default is very much turning to the higher voltage.

Eight hundred volts is presented as a leap forward, and in one sense it is.

But it’s also arguably a tad over-hyped, at least for the vast majority of the time for most EV owners.

What 800V really means

An EV battery is a stack of individual cells wired together.

Each cell typically puts out somewhere around 3.6 volts for NMC (nickel manganese cobalt) batteries, or around 3.2V for LFP (lithium ferrous phosphate) batteries.

Wire them in series and the voltages add up; wire them in parallel and the capacity adds up.

They’ll still have the same amount of energy, but how they absorb and disperse it can be different.

Arrange them one way and you get a pack of around 400V, which is what most EVs have utilised until recently.

Arrange them another way and you can step the voltage up to 800 or more.

Even then, the voltage an EV puts out varies depending on how much charge is in the battery.

And the voltage is rarely 800V.

The Porsche Taycan is the car that started it all, yet even though it’s badged as an 800-volt system the original cars had a nominal voltage of 613V for the smaller battery and 723V for the larger battery.

And for that larger battery the voltage can swing from about 610 volts when flat to about 835 volts when full.

Voltage rises as state of charge rises, which is how the car monitors how much charge is left.

So an 800V system is not so much a hard and fast measurement, in the same way the 12V batteries used in all cars rarely put out 12 volts; they usually hover around  12.6 volts and get pushed to 14V or higher when the car is running.

When you see claims of how fast a car can charge it will often be relying on a high voltage – in the case of the upcoming Porsche Cayenne that’s 850V – and a lot of current (the amps required to get the power up).

Voltage ain’t power, but it helps achieve it

Anyone who remembers their high school physics will know that electrical power equals voltage multiplied by amps.

Ultimately, it’s the power that determines how fast the car will charge – but a higher voltage makes it easier to produce more power.

If you want to push 350kW into a battery at 400V, you need 875 amps. That’s a lot.

Push the same 350kW at 800V and you need less than 440 amps.

Compare that with the 10A maximum that a home powerpoint can put out and you can see we’re talking about big hits of electricity.

And those amps – the current – is the problem.

Current generates heat, and heat is the enemy of everything in the charging chain: including the cables and various connectors.

That’s why high-power charging cables can be liquid-cooled and very thick (and, therefore, heavy).

Double the current and you quadruple the resistive losses. Halve it and those losses drop off a cliff.

So doubling the voltage lets you move a lot more energy through the same hardware.

The main benefit with 800V is DC fast charging

An 800V architecture is almost entirely about public DC fast charging.

It affects almost nothing else with your ownership experience.

Charging at home on AC is identical no matter what the voltage of the battery pack.

Your home powerpoint – or EV charger – puts out about 230V, which is a whole heap less than what the battery is rated at.

It also goes through the car’s onboard charger to convert it from AC electricity coming out of the wall to DC electricity to be stored in the battery pack.

That onboard charger is typically 7kW, 11kW or 22kW, regardless of pack voltage.

An 800V Hyundai Ioniq 5 and a 400V Tesla Model Y plugged into the same wallbox overnight will do exactly the same thing at exactly the same rate.

For anyone charging predominantly at home – which is most EV owners, most of the time – 800V is a number on a brochure.

However, there are some secondary benefits.

Lower current means thinner cables and less copper inside the car, which saves a few kilograms and some cost.

For Porsche, the lower weight is important.

It’s a company that has built its reputation on performance, so every little bit counts.

Higher voltages also mean slightly lower losses under sustained high load.

That’s one reason electricity is transported at extremely high voltages (sometimes 500,000V) over big distances.

For Porsche and others chasing big performance, the higher voltage can help with repeatable track performance rather than just charging.

Really, though, the headline is faster charging.

Are there downsides to an 800V electrical system?

Higher voltage is harder and more expensive to engineer.

Every high-voltage component – inverters, DC-DC converters, compressors, contactors, insulation, connectors – has to be rated for the extra stress.

Silicon carbide semiconductors rated to 1200V are one solution, but they cost more than those used in a 400V EV.

Higher voltages also mean greater insulation to ensure safety.

And the big one: if the charger you’re using is limited to 400V then there’s zero benefit.

In some instances there could be negatives.

Roll up to the latest 300kW Tesla Supercharger, for example, and the limiting factor could be the current (amp) limit on the car.

The Hyundai Ioniq 5/6/9 are a good example.

Their DC charging typically tops out at about 320kW, which is 400A of current.

The cabling in the car, therefore, is limited to 400A, which at 400V is 160kW.

Similarly, the Porsche Macan is rated at up to 270kW of fast charging, but only on 800V. At 400V it’s limited to 135kW, again due to those current limits.

So even though the cars are capable of higher-powered charging, it relies on the 800V system to achieve that.

Can an 800V EV use a 400V charger?

All EVs can use all fast chargers, no matter what the voltage of the charger or what voltage the car is rated at.

That’s thanks to some simple but clever designs that allow the electrons to sort themselves out and everything to work as intended.

But there are different ways of achieving it.

The simplest way – and the way used by the Porsche Taycan, Audi e-tron and latest Mercedes-Benz CLA – is to use a DC-to-DC booster.

It steps the voltage up so that the battery sees 800V.

With its latest Macan, Porsche did without the need for that booster, instead essentially splitting the battery into two 400V banks and charging them concurrently when it sees a 400V load.

Hyundai and Kia used something quite clever, employing the motor as an inverter.

The rear inverter is reconfigured to act as a boost converter and the rear motor’s windings do the job of the inductor.

So there’s no additional hardware, no extra weight, although presumably there’s some tricky software to ensure it all works the way it should.

800V charging is limited, for now

Here’s where the enthusiasm needs tempering.

Australia’s ultra-rapid network – the 350kW and 450kW units from the likes of Evie, Chargefox, NRMA, Ampol and BP – will generally deliver above 800V and let an 800V EV maximise its charging speed.

But the far bigger slice of Australia’s public charging infrastructure is 400V, often limited to 50kW and 75kW hardware.

That includes the vast Tesla Supercharger network, much of it now open to all EVs.

That’s because all Teslas sold in Australia run a 400V system (the Cybertruck is the brand’s first 800V EV).

Tesla’s reasoning is that bigger, higher-draw vehicles benefit, smaller EVs with smaller batteries less so.

The other half of the answer is that Tesla built its way around the problem. Rather than raising voltage, it went hard on current: Model 3 and Model Y peak at 250kW on a 400V system.

Tesla owns its charging network, so it had the advantage of being able to optimise both ends of the equation.

Is it inevitable Tesla changes? Probably, but it’ll likely happen when a new platform demands it.

Why not go to 1000V or 2000V?

Higher voltage is generally better, right?

In many instances, yes, but it also creates challenges.

BYD’s Super e-Platform is a full 1000V architecture, paired with a battery capable of charging at up to 1000A, for a peak of 1000kW.

That’s the tech behind the “flash charging” sites Denza has committed to installing at Australian dealerships.

So, if 800 is better than 400, why isn’t everyone at 1500V or higher?

Essentially it comes down to safety.

We’ve all seen lightning, which is a high voltage burst of electricity travelling through thin air.

Air is an insulator, but only up to a point.

Push enough voltage across a gap and the air itself ionises and becomes conductive – you get an arc.

The higher the voltage, the wider the gap it can jump.

No amount of clever software gets around it.

Engineers solve the issue by providing more clearance – distance – between high voltage components where you don’t want a spark.

Go higher in voltage and components have to physically move further apart, in a car where nobody has spare room.

There’s also the issue of the plug.

The CCS2 Combo plug fitted to every EV now sold in Australia – including Teslas – tops out at 1000V.

Anything beyond means a new connector standard, which the EV world (rightly) is not in a rush to adopt.

Components dealing with higher voltages can also get expensive.

Besides, with circa-300km charging now down to 10 minutes or less – and BYD/Denza’s flash charging to halve that – it’s getting to the point where the gains are minimal.

Will all brands end up on 800V?

More and more cars are embracing 800V electrical systems, but not because 800V is magic.

It’ll happen because new platforms get designed once and live for a decade, because silicon carbide is getting cheaper every year, and because no car maker wants to be the one whose spec sheet says 400 when the rival’s says 800.

With bigger and more luxurious EVs it’s a no-brainer to head to 800V.

But we’d still expect cheaper city-focussed cars to stay 400V for a while yet, because an LFP hatchback with a 50kWh battery charging at 80kW has nothing to gain.

One point worth making is :don’t go buying an EV based on the voltage.

Buy it because of how it suits your needs and if the charging achieves what you need it to in terms of time taken.

A car that hits 350kW for 90 seconds and then falls off a cliff is not as good as one that sits at 180kW from 10 to 70 per cent.

data.title: Volkswagen turns iconic GTI on its head: Electric ID.3 is first rear-drive GTI and the most powerful ever
data.description:
One of the most famous performance badges in motoring is undergoing its biggest transformation yet, with Volkswagen revealing the electric ID.3 GTI as the first rear-wheel-drive GTI and the most powerful production model in the badge’s 50-year history.

The new battery-electric hot hatch develops 240kW and 545Nm and sends all of it to the rear wheels – a dramatic departure for a badge that has been synonymous with front-wheel-drive performance since the original Golf GTI appeared in 1976.

Volkswagen says the ID.3 GTI will accelerate from 0-100km/h in 5.6 seconds, while top speed is electronically limited to 200km/h.

READ MORE: https://evcentral.com.au/re-hatched-why-the-overhauled-volkswagen-id-3-neo-might-finally-have-everything-it-needs-to-do-well-in-australia-and-beat-the-tesla-model-3-and-mg4/
READ MORE: Volkswagen ID. Polo GTI performance numbers confirmed: Heavier and slower than ICE but VW guarantees great handling
READ MORE: 6.48kWh/100km! Volkswagen Mission Efficiency electric car shows how frugal an EV can be in the real world

Its 240kW output also edges past the 239kW Golf GTI Edition 50, making the electric model the most powerful series-production GTI Volkswagen has produced.

The transformation is significant because GTI has spent five decades closely associated with the Golf and, subsequently, other front-drive Volkswagens including the Polo.

The original 81kW 1976 Golf GTI helped establish the modern hot-hatch formula by combining relatively affordable performance with the practicality of a small family hatchback.

Volkswagen is now attempting to carry that philosophy into its electric range.

The ID.3 GTI is not the first electric Volkswagen to be associated with the GTI badge – an ID. Polo GTI is also part of the company’s new-generation EV program – but it is the first rear-wheel-drive GTI.

Its electric motor is integrated into the rear axle and draws power from a 79kWh usable lithium-ion battery.

Volkswagen claims a WLTP driving range of up to 601km and energy consumption of 14.5kWh/100km, although both figures remain forecasts ahead of production.

Maximum DC charging power is 183kW, with a claimed 10-80 per cent recharge taking about 29 minutes.

But Volkswagen is placing at least as much emphasis on making the ID.3 feel like a GTI as it is on outright performance.

Standard equipment includes an adaptive DCC sports chassis, direct progressive steering, launch control and a dedicated GTI driving mode.

Pressing a GTI button on the steering wheel switches the powertrain, steering and adaptive chassis to their sportiest settings, activates launch control availability and changes the cabin lighting and digital instruments to a red GTI theme.

Intriguingly, it also introduces the sound of a combustion engine into the cabin – part of Volkswagen’s attempt to give the electric hot hatch some of the character traditionally associated with petrol-powered GTIs.

The exterior carries plenty of familiar GTI references as well.

A red strip runs across the nose in a direct reference to the red grille surround of the original 1976 Golf GTI, while the car gains a black honeycomb lower grille, GTI-specific bumper treatment and standard 20-inch Wörthersee alloy wheels – themselves named after the Austrian location famous for hosting the annual GTI gathering.

Inside, the traditional GTI tartan seat pattern has been reinterpreted for the electric model, while there is red stitching, a red 12 o’clock steering-wheel marker and GTI-specific digital instrumentation.

Underneath all that is Volkswagen’s extensively updated ID.3 Neo, which introduces a substantially revised interior including a 12.9-inch infotainment screen and, notably, the return of more physical controls.

There are separate climate-control switches below the touchscreen and a rotary controller on the centre console for audio volume and track selection.

The ID.3 GTI also offers vehicle-to-load capability through an optional adapter connected to its charging port, allowing the battery to power or recharge external electrical equipment.

European pre-sales are scheduled to begin in early 2027. Unfortunately, Australian GTI enthusiasts shouldn’t start saving just yet.

The regular ID.3 has never reached Australia despite previously being earmarked for local sale, and Volkswagen Australia has increasingly concentrated its electric-car efforts on SUVs.

The company’s current Australian EV passenger-car range centres on the ID.4 and ID.5 SUVs, while Volkswagen Australia executives have previously pointed to this country’s strong preference for SUVs when discussing the business case for smaller electric hatchbacks such as the ID.3 Neo.

That makes an Australian launch for the ID.3 GTI unlikely under current plans, although Volkswagen has not formally ruled out the latest ID.3 generation.

There is nevertheless some Australian precedent for its mechanical layout. The closely related Cupra Born has previously been sold here, although the updated version has yet to be confirmed for a local return.

The post Volkswagen turns iconic GTI on its head: Electric ID.3 is first rear-drive GTI and the most powerful ever appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Another potential electric ute for Australia? Geely’s new Riddara King Kong EV takes aim at workhorse market
data.description:
Geely has revealed an updated version of its affordable King Kong electric ute in China as the Australian market finally starts warming up to battery-powered pick-ups.

Shown at the Chengdu motor show under Geely’s domestic Radar brand, the 2026 King Kong EV adds a lower-range work-focused model while offering up to 605km of claimed range, four-wheel drive and almost one-tonne payload capacity further up the range.

And it has obvious Australian relevance. Radar is known as Riddara in export markets, while versions of the King Kong are closely related to the RD6 ute Geely has previously earmarked for Australia.

READ MORE: On the radar: 2024 Riddara RD6 electric ute confirmed for Australia as zero-emission Ford Ranger, Toyota Hilux rival
READ MORE: Geely reveals Radar RD6 dual-cab ute, first model from new global EV brand
READ MORE: Another challenger for Toyota Camry: Geely Emgrand L EM-i PHEV confirmed for Australia in 2027

Geely has so far prioritised a plug-in hybrid version of its next Riddara ute for Australia rather than a pure EV, but the arrival of new battery-powered rivals including the MG U9 EV and Toyota HiLux EV could potentially change that thinking.

The latest King Kong EV range spans rear- and four-wheel drive, standard- and long-wheelbase bodies and multiple battery capacities.

The cheapest work-focused version introduced around the Chengdu show is aimed squarely at commercial users, trading maximum driving range for a lower purchase price.

Geely’s current Chinese specifications list a 42kWh lithium iron phosphate battery with 310km of CLTC range for the entry rear-drive long-wheelbase model, while Chengdu material also detailed a 370km commercial version.

Further up the range, 63kWh, 73kWh and 86kWh batteries extend claimed CLTC range as far as 605km.

Rear-drive versions produce 180kW and 309Nm, while the dual-motor four-wheel-drive King Kong steps up to 280kW and 485Nm.

Geely claims the latter can accelerate from 0-100km/h in 5.7 seconds when empty and 7.8 seconds fully loaded.

Payload is one of the more interesting numbers for Australia. Rear-drive models are rated to carry up to 790kg, while four-wheel-drive versions increase that to 910kg – putting the King Kong closer to traditional working utes than lifestyle-oriented electric pick-ups.

Standard-wheelbase versions measure about 5.26 metres long with a 3120mm wheelbase and 1525mm-long tray, while the long-wheelbase stretches to about 5.5 metres, with a 3310mm wheelbase and 1765mm tray.

The King Kong is built on Geely’s M.A.P architecture developed specifically for new-energy pick-ups and uses independent suspension rather than the traditional ladder-frame and leaf-spring layout familiar from diesel workhorses.

The Chengdu update also brings Flyme Auto 2 infotainment, centred around a 14.6-inch touchscreen.

More unusual is the ute’s ability to function as a substantial mobile power source. Geely offers 220V output from the regular charging port as well as high-voltage external discharge designed to power equipment, machinery and even charge agricultural drones.

The company quotes up to 30kW directly from the fast-charge connection, with Chengdu demonstrations showcasing external power capability of up to 36kW when the broader system is used.

Pricing demonstrates how aggressively Geely is positioning its electric ute in China. The broader King Kong EV family currently starts from 99,800 yuan – about $21,000 on a simple currency conversion – with higher-specification versions extending to 159,800 yuan, or about $A34,000.

An Australian launch for the King Kong EV has not been on the public agenda. Geely previously told Australian media its priority was an all-new Riddara PHEV rather than bringing the existing battery-electric RD6 here, reflecting the stronger local demand for electrified utes that can still travel long distances without charging.

A larger PHEV V6 ute has also been reported as coming to Australia.

The post Another potential electric ute for Australia? Geely’s new Riddara King Kong EV takes aim at workhorse market appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: 6.48kWh/100km! Volkswagen Mission Efficiency electric car shows how frugal an EV can be in the real world
data.description:
Volkswagen has built an ultra-efficient electric prototype capable of travelling more than 1200km while consuming less than half the energy of many current EVs – and much of the technology underneath it is headed for affordable production cars.

Called the Volkswagen Mission Efficiency, the streamlined 2+2-seat coupe has achieved a claimed aerodynamic drag coefficient of just 0.158 and averaged 6.89kWh/100km during a 1278km European road trip.

More importantly for future Volkswagen EV buyers, the concept isn’t based around an exotic experimental drivetrain.

READ MORE: Volkswagen crisis: Cheap Chinese EVs, Trump’s tariffs, high costs, low profits and technical missteps hit German car giant hard
READ MORE: Volkswagen ID. Cross arrives: T-Cross-replacing SUV switches to EV power to beat the BYD Atto 2, Geely EX2 and MG S5
READ MORE: 2026 Volkswagen Tayron eHybrid Review: VW’s other plug-in SUV might be the smarter Tiguan

Its 99kW electric motor, 54.9kWh usable battery and front-wheel-drive architecture are derived from the MEB+ technology being introduced in the Volkswagen ID. Polo and ID. Cross.

Volkswagen says the Mission Efficiency has established three records covering aerodynamics, controlled-condition energy consumption and real-world efficiency.

During an officially documented 1278.36km journey from Volkswagen’s Wolfsburg development centre in Germany through Poland and the Czech Republic to Vienna, Austria, it averaged 6.89kWh/100km excluding charging losses. Including those losses, consumption was 7.51kWh/100km.

The car averaged 67.72km/h and reached a maximum speed of 138km/h during the journey. Its 54.9kWh battery required only one recharge and Volkswagen says the Mission Efficiency still indicated 164km of remaining range when it arrived in Vienna.

In a separate controlled test at a constant 68km/h, with no gradients and ancillary systems including climate control switched off, consumption fell to 6.48kWh/100km.

The numbers underline how much additional EV range can potentially be extracted without simply installing a larger and heavier battery. Aerodynamics are central to the result.

Volkswagen chief designer Andreas Mindt says the car’s functional shape draws inspiration from the Volkswagen XL1, the two-seat diesel plug-in hybrid launched in limited production in 2013.

The Mission Efficiency combines its 0.158 drag coefficient with a small 2.08-square-metre frontal area. Its body uses a teardrop profile along with active cooling flaps, covered rear wheels, a fully enclosed underbody, frameless windows and flush door handles.

Volkswagen claims that above 80km/h the prototype consumes more than 30 per cent less energy than the production ID. Polo. At 140km/h, it is claimed to require approximately the same amount of energy as the ID. Polo does at 100km/h.

The wheels received particular attention because Volkswagen estimates they contribute 25-30 per cent of a vehicle’s aerodynamic resistance.

Closely fitted front wheelarches are combined with patented deflectors inside each wheel designed to prevent airflow entering the rims and generating turbulence. Flat aerodynamic wheel covers are fitted externally.

Volkswagen also worked with Continental on special tyres based on the EcoContact 7. Their claimed rolling resistance of 4.9kg per tonne is around 25 per cent below the threshold required for the European Union’s highest Class A tyre rating.

There are further efficiency gains from a 370-watt photovoltaic system incorporated into the glass roof and rear window.

Rather than directly powering the propulsion system, the solar installation supplies the car’s electrical accessories. Volkswagen claims it could contribute the equivalent of up to 30km of additional driving range per day depending on weather, season and location.

Weight has also been attacked. The Mission Efficiency combines some ID. Polo components with a self-supporting aluminium structure and parts manufactured from carbon fibre-reinforced polymer and aramid composite materials.

Its minimalist cabin deletes a conventional infotainment display in favour of the driver’s smartphone or tablet, while even the normal audio system has been replaced by a portable Bluetooth speaker.

Despite the efficiency focus, Volkswagen says the Mission Efficiency has been designed as a potentially usable vehicle rather than simply a record-breaking streamliner.

It measures 4775mm long but only 1392mm high and provides four seats, although the rear pair are only intended for occupants up to approximately 1.60 metres tall.

Boot capacity is a substantial 481 litres, supplemented by storage areas beneath the rear seats and within the sides of the body.

There are also some potentially production-relevant developments underneath. The Mission Efficiency retains the ID. Polo’s MacPherson front suspension and hydraulic front brakes but introduces an electromechanical rear braking system developed with automotive supplier Aumovio.

Volkswagen says eliminating hydraulic components at the rear reduces friction, plumbing and brake fluid requirements while allowing variable brake-force distribution. That can improve regenerative braking as well as cornering stability.

The prototype has received European road approval and Volkswagen says it complies with the associated safety, structural and crash requirements.

While there is no suggestion Volkswagen intends putting the Mission Efficiency itself into production, the company is positioning it as a development exercise demonstrating how far EV efficiency can be pushed using components closely related to mainstream models.

The post 6.48kWh/100km! Volkswagen Mission Efficiency electric car shows how frugal an EV can be in the real world appeared first on EV Central.
